prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how reallocation of resources across firms shapes the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) shifted the unit of analysis in trade from the industry to the firm. It shows that selection into exporting and reallocation toward more productive firms are a distinct source of aggregate productivity gains. The result is general, and it has been tested against firm-level data in many countries for more than twenty years. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exports versus FDI, together with his wider program on trade and firm organisation, supports a joint credit. The idea also reaches beyond trade. It is part of the micro-to-macro link between firm dynamics, reallocation and aggregate productivity that runs through modern growth and productivity research. After hearing colleagues, I now put this entry first. I ranked B001 first in my opening, but several colleagues made points that lower my confidence in it relative to B005. The work is more recent, the credit-supply versus other-channel debate is still open, and it overlaps with the 2022 prize. B005 is older and more tested, its attribution is cleaner, and its distinction from earlier prizes is easier to state.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum contributed closely related empirical and theoretical work, and none of them is among the credited names, so a Helpman-Melitz citation may overstate the priority of that pair. A second concern is overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize. Helpman's earlier new trade theory work sits in the lineage Krugman was recognised for, so Helpman's marginal credit rests mainly on the heterogeneous-firm extensions. Some welfare conclusions also depend on functional-form assumptions, such as Pareto productivity and CES demand.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B011 first. He argues that Kiyotaki-Moore is the clean originator of the collateral-price feedback mechanism, that the 2007-09 crisis tested it, and that timing is ripe. He limits the credit to the two originators because Bernanke and Gertler were partly recognised in 2022.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity. Kiyotaki-Moore is a clearly two-author, well-confirmed contribution, and I keep B011 as my first alternative. I ranked it seventh in my opening mainly because of the overlap with 2022. That overlap concerns the broader accelerator lineage more than the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism, so his narrow framing partly answers my worry. I still put B005 ahead. Its empirical record in firm-level data is more direct, whereas the identification of the quantitative size of the collateral channel is more indirect. I would not treat B011 as a weaker case on merit, however. The choice between them seems closer to me than my opening ranks suggest.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B005 fourth. She notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are missing from the credited names, that Krugman's earlier prize recognised the new trade theory tradition, and that some welfare conclusions are sensitive to functional-form assumptions.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution concern, and it is my main reservation. It cannot be fully resolved from the credited names, so I would keep the citation worded around the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection, not around the empirical discovery of exporter premia. That wording fits Melitz's 2003 model and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension, and it avoids claiming the empirical priority that belongs to others. On Krugman, I read Melitz's step as distinct. Krugman's work explains trade through scale economies and love of variety, whereas Melitz explains welfare gains through selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms. On functional-form sensitivity I concede the point. The core selection mechanism is robust, but the size of the gains depends on the structure. This is a reason to word the citation carefully, not a reason to reject the entry.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B011 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He argues that Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the financial-accelerator strand, which overlaps with the work recognised in 2022. He ranks B005 third, with Helpman and Melitz as the core pair and Redding's quantitative contribution as later and more specialised.
responses.response: I agree with his two-name core for B005. Redding's quantitative and spatial work extends the framework and is not part of the originating insight, so I keep him out. On B011 I find his argument for excluding Gertler and Gilchrist persuasive, and I would not add a third name there either. Our difference is mainly about which entry comes first. I weigh B005 more because the firm-level evidence is more direct. I accept that this is a judgment call, and I would not oppose B011 in a configuration with the same level of attribution care.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first. He stresses that the heterogeneous-firm framework is general, that it has more than two decades of confirmation, and that it underpins a large empirical and policy literature. He also notes that Krugman's 2008 prize and Helpman's separate protection-for-sale work (B020) leave some overlap and ambiguity in the credit.
responses.response: I share his view of the generality and maturity of the framework. The B020 overlap is a real ambiguity, but it does not affect the proposed citation. The citation rests only on the firm-heterogeneity contributions, and Helpman's credit for those is already independent of the protection-for-sale work. I would not make a second part out of Helpman's other contributions. That would break the three-person limit and dilute a clear achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will credit Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not among the listed names, in a way that weakens the Helpman-Melitz pairing.
How much marginal credit Helpman has beyond the lineage covered by Krugman's 2008 prize, and how the overlap with his separate B020 entry is to be handled.
Whether the 2022 overlap concern for B011 and B001 is stronger than I judge, which would raise the relative position of B005.

Because of the three-person limit across the whole configuration, a two-part prize cannot combine B005 with B011 without dropping a name on one side. I therefore propose a single part, and that choice is a judgment about the strength of each case.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile shows frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary) and co-authorship with John Hassler (chair), and both are IIES colleagues. I also have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow, who is credited in B016. B016 is not in my preferred configuration, and I ranked it sixth in the opening, with that disclosure. I also have collaborations with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li on creative destruction and growth measurement, which relates thematically to firm-productivity work but not to the credited names in B005. The profile shows no direct connection to Helpman, Melitz or Redding, so none is apparent for the preferred part. The profile suggests I may have helped draft the 2025 Scientific Background, but that is weak evidence and has no bearing on this ballot. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
